ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Resumption of Indo-Pak Talks 
* 161. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: SHRI SANTOSH 
BAGRODIA: 
Will the Minister of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether United States wants India and Pakistan to resume talks and resolve the protracted 
Kashmir conflict and put back on trade the derailed Lahore peace process; and 
(b) if so, Government's reaction thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): (a) There is no 
US mediation on Indo-Pak talks. However, the US side has expressed a hope for the resumption of 
Indo-Pak talks. The US side has also reiterated its position, as articulated by President Clinton, namely 
urging restraint, respect for Line of Control, refraining from violence and for renewed lines of 
communication. In this context, the US side ha s urged Pakistan to create conditions for a 
meaningful dialogue to take place. The US Government has also stated publicly on a number of 
occasions, including on 7th July 2000, that it does not seek the role of a mediator between India and 
Pakistan. 
(b) Government believes that all outstanding issues between India and Pakistan should be 
resolved peacefully through bilateral dialogue. It is Government's position that Pakistan must 
create appropriate conditions for the dialogue to start, by stopping its sponsorship of and support to 
cross-border terrorism in India. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir I would like to be educated with regard to the first line of 
the answer... 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: You are highly educated. 
The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri Ghulam Nabi Azad. 
1 

 RAJYA SABHA [3rd August, 2000] 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Not in the field of diplomacy, at least, and that too 
while discussing with your party. It is stated, There is no US mediation on Indo-Pak talks." 
Sir, part (a) of my question is this. Th e Minister might have gone through newspaper 
reports, as everybody has,—that even today's newspapers have reported—that US President 
Bill Clinton has informed our Prime Minister that he is going to talk to the Pakistani leaders 
or the leadership of Pakistan to support the peace talks. So, I would like to know from the 
hon. Foreign Minister as to how does he explain this unusual interest on the part of the United 
States, and how does he say that there is no mediation? That is why I said in the beginning 
that I would like to be educat ed about the meaning of the wo rd mediation'. If this is not 
mediation, then what is mediation? 
Sir, part (b) of my question is this, I would tike to know from the hon. Foreign 
Minister whether he is aware of the fact th at a study group sponsored by one. of the US-
based think-tanks has proposed trifurcation of the State of Jammu and Kashmir. If so, what 
is the response of the Government of India in this regard? 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, even though the Question 
Hour is not an educational class, I would endeavour to explain the matter. I will not go into 
the dictionary meaning of the word 'mediation' . It is clear enough. Mediation means, two 
sides, and the third party sitting as some kind of a Panch. Wc have seen in other instances. 
In our neighbourhood, for example; the repres entative of Norway attempting to clear the 
road between the LTTE and the Sri Lankan Government. 
In this case, as recently as on 7th July, in  response to a specific question, the United 
States Government, through its spokesman, stated, "We do not see ourselves as a mediator." 
Expression of hope, concern about international de velopments, situation is very different to 
playing a mediatory role. Like, for example, the United States expressing the hope in regard 
to developments in South Asia, India expressing the hope in regard to developments in Sri 
Lanka, or for that mailer, the West Asian peace talks. This does not mean a mediatory role. It 
is a part of the expression of concern which most international organisations or bodies or 
countries indulge in. Therefore, there should be no ambiguity in this regard. Of course, 
there is no ambiguity. As far as Government of India's response to a study in the USA, 
recommending one course or another, in regard to the Indian State of Jammu & Kashmir, is 
concerned, let me inform the hon. Member that we do not pay heed to studies. 
2 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
They are free to carry out whatever stud ies they wish to carry out. A number 
of institutions in India car ry out academic studies on a variety of international 
situations. That, in no way, either influences or affects the Government of 
India's thinking on policy in regard to  absolute clarity with regard to the 
Indian State of Jammu & Kashmir. Again, I say, Sir, there is no ambiguity in 
this respect  
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir, there is a dichotomy between what the Foreign Ministry 
says and what the U.S. does. The hon. Foreign Minister has cited the example of Norway and Sri 
Lanka. I am not aware of the fact whether they are in favour of a third party intervention or not. But 
as far as India is concerned, the consistent policy, even when our Government was in power, has 
been that there shall not be any third party intervention. So, we cite the examples of other countries. 
They might have accepted third party intervention officially, and they are inviting them. I do not 
think this is an example which can be cited, as far as our country is concerned. 
As far as the second part of the question is concerned, the nation is proud of our soldiers 
who made supreme sacrifice for the security and territorial integrity of our country while fighting 
the Pakistanis at Kargil. But, Sir, subsequent to that, the Government, in general, and the Home 
Minister, Shri L.K. Advani, in particular, in this very House said, "Kargil victory was qualitatively 
superior to the victory of 1971 as India has not only won in the battlefield but also in the diplomatic 
field. "Sir, it is good enough. I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Foreign Minister to what 
the U.S. President, Bill Clinton, said while addressing the joint sitting of Members of Parliament in 
March, 2000: "I have certainly not come to South Asia to mediate the dispute over Kashmir. Only 
India and Pakistan can work out the problems between them and I will say the same thing to General 
Musharraf in Islamabad." To this extent it is okay. Now I quote the operative part: "If outsiders 
can't resolve this problem, I hope, you will create the opportunity to do it yourselves, calling on the 
support of others who can help, where possible, as American diplomacy did in urging the Pakistanis to 
go back behind the line of control in Kargil crisis." 
I would like to inform the hon. Minister that the Government is now trying to take credit for 
international diplomacy saying that for the first time, in fifty years, we have such a diplomacy that we 
can win the support of the whole world. I would like to know from the hon. Foreign Minister whether 
this was a victory for U.S. diplomacy or a victory of the Indian diplomacy. 
Thank you. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [3rd August, 2000] 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Mr. Chairman, Sir, there are two parts of it. One is this 
that there seems to be some misunderstanding in the hon. Member's mind about what I cited as 
an example between interests, expression of interests and mediation; and when I cited the 
example of Norway playing a role in Sri Lanka, it is not to suggest that there  is any role 
being played here of any similar or corresponding kind, and arrange third party intervention 
in India's internal affairs or particularly in the case of management of the situation in the 
Indian State of Jammu and Kashmir, let there be no ambiguity or doubt in the hon. 
Member's mind. The second question really does not arise from the 
US aspect. The suggestion ........... {Interruptions)... I will answer it. Do not worry. 
Do not be impatient. It does not strictly arise because the hon. Member's question really 
relates to the US mediation. And what the hon. Member has done is  to stretch the US 
mediations cite the visit of the US President wherein he said, "We are not mediating." And 
thereafter he said, "We did have a role to play on leaning on Pakistan and urging them to 
withdraw beyond the line of control." On that the hon. Member wants me to explain whether 
it was a success of Indian diplomacy or US diplomacy. I am not in a competition game. The 
reality is for the world to see; the reality is for India to see. And if persuaded by partisanship or 
political consideration, the hon. Member wishes to derive some different interpretation to 
the interpretation that we have, he is perfectly free to do so. 
SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD: Sir, I take strong objection to the words used by the 
hon. Minister because this is something which the President of the United States said while 
addressing the Members of Parliament, the Indian Parliament. As a Parliamentarian, I could 
not put this question to the US President. It is  the Foreign Minister who has to reply to this 
question because while addressing the Parliament , he said, "It was at our instance that it 
was done." Instead of accepting that, they cried hoarse, "we, we, we". They should 
have accepted it ......... (Interruptions)... Now they are blaming us that it is partisan 
attitude. ...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI M. VENKAIAH NAIDU: "We, we, we," and everybody knows it. 
...(Interruptions)... 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Mr. Chairman, Sir, I will go a step further than my 
colleague. The second sentence of his reply is, "However, the US side has expressed a hope 
for the resumption of Indo-Pak talks." I am not going further on this. But the last sentence 
of the first paragraph says," ..it doe s not seek the role of a mediator between India and 
Pakistan." I wish if you had added, "unless bot h agree" because this was the attitude of the 
US President 
4 

[3rd August, 2000} RAJYA SABHA 
also. Addressing the National Committee of the Democratic Party at a dinner -meeting in 
Baltimore before leaving for India, he said, "We are working on the peace processes, from 
Northern Ireland to the Middle East, and I am going to the Indian subcontinent at the end of

SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, there are two different questions here. First, "has the 
US ever offered mediatory role", the reply is  quite clear, Sir, No. Secondly, "Has the 
suggestion been made that Pakistan be declar ed as a terrorist State" On a number of 
occasions public statements have been made in this regard that demonstrable action by the 
Government of "Pakistan and the support that it continues to lend to cross border terrorism 
warrants such an action bei ng taken. No formal request, however, through diplomatic 
channels, has ever been made.

SHRI NILOTPAL BASU: Sir, through you, I draw the attention of the 
hon. External Affairs Minister to (b) part of the reply. The-Government believes that all 
outstanding issues between India and Pakist an should be resolved peacefully through 
bilateral dialogue. It is Government's position that Pakistan must create appropriate 
conditions for the dialogue to start by stopping  its sponsorship and suppart to terrorism in 
India. Now, even the latest incident 
5 

RAJYA SABHA                                            [3rd August, 2000] 
of day-before-yesterday shows that there is no re lenting so far as Pakistan is concerned, in 
the sponsoring of cross border terrorism. Here , it is good to see that the Government is 
reiterating the position that there wouid be no third party mediation. Therefore, the question 
that is agitating not only me but the whol e country is, how to go about in trying to 
normalise the situation in Kashmir. Opening a channel of dialogue only with the Hizbul 
Mujahideen will not suffice because experts sa y that a bulk of the terrorists are actually 
being controlled by the group which is close to the Pakistan leadership and Pakistan 
Government. How to go about it? What are the plans? If the External Affairs Minister is kind 
enough, he can give a broad road map of what is our t h i n k i n g  at this point of time. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, this question has been answered just yesterday by the 
hon. Home Minister. It is, of course, a collective and joint 
effort by the Home Ministry and the Ministry of Defence as also the Ministry of External 
Affairs. It is very clear, Sir, that we have to be absolutely unflinching in our resolve, firstly, 
to defeat terrorism of any and all variety in the State of Jammu and Kashmir or elsewhere in 
the Republic of India. Secondly, Sir, we have to be committed to the path of peace 
unwaveringly and constantly, never shy of progressing with any step that will lead to peace, 
not simply in the State of Jammu and Kashmir,  but in other parts of India as well, and, 
thirdly, so far as internal management goes, as my colleag ue, the Union Home Minister, 
informed the House yesterday, the Government and all must address themselve to issues that 
generate discontent within our citizens as for example issues relating to unemployment, lack 
of income, issues of that variety. Internationally, Sir I do make bold to assert that it is only 
after the Kargil mis-adventure of Pakistan that cross-border terrorism or international 
terrorism has now come to the forefront on the international agenda and features not si mp l y  
in the bilateral talks that India has but it is featuring in the statements that are being issued 
from a variety of international bodies the U.N. the G-8 Countries, and in the recently held 
meeting of the ARF, in Bangkok. And, in that regard, 1 am quite happy to inform the hon. 
Member that India is sponsoring, in the fo rthcoming U.N. General Assembly Meeting, a 
comprehensive convention on i n t er n a t i o n a l  terrorism and we have already received a fairly 
widespread support in this regard. 
SHRI S. VIDUTHALAI VIRUMBI: Mr. Chairman, Sir, the President of the USA, as 
per reports in the media, had talks with our  Prime Minister over telephone regarding the 
indiscriminate firing at the Amarnath Yatris. Th is itself clearly shows that this is the result 
of the diplomatic exercise by 
6 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SAB HA 
our External Affairs Ministry. We  feel it is a victory for the Government of India. In this 
context,, what I feel is,, mediation is totall y different from informal  consultations with 
countries. Therefore, what I would like to know after the visit of the President, Mr. Clinton, 
to India of course, subsequently, he had been to Pakistan, though it was a short visit 
whether the Government of India has received any feedback from the President of the USA 
regarding the cross-border terrorism being indulged in by Pakistan. Whether any advice has 
been given to Pakistan by the USA? Have we received any feedback from the USA? If yes; 
what action has so far been taken by the Govern ment of India or what action is proposed to 
be taken by the Government of India? Thank you. 
SHRI JASWANT SINGH: Sir, Yes. We have,, as the hon. Member knows, announced 
one of the decisions during President Clinton's visit to India. In fact, implemented just 
before that, was the decision with regard to establishing a Joint Working Group on terrorism 
between USA and India. That Joint Working Group has already held two meetings and there is a 
fair degree of co-operation exchange of information on many items, including and 
particularly, cross-border terrorism. Just be fore coming here, I was made available a 
statement that has been formally issued by the U.S. Government about the outrage 
committed against humanity if I may say so. I would not read out the whole thing. The 
statement says "The wanton acts of inhumanity are clearly aimed at  undermining the cease-
fire declared last week by the Hazibul Mu jahideen and the Indian security forces. We 
condemn these outrageous and inhuman massa cres. We extend our deep-felt condolences 
and welcome the statement of the Indian Prime Minister that India will continue to pursue 
the path of peace." We constantly keep in t ouch with other countries;  not simply the USA. 
Now, in regard to cross-border terrorism for example there is a close working between India 
and the Russian Federation and also a number of Central Asian Countries. Therefore, on the 
issue of cross-border terrorism there is a much greater recognition and awareness in the 
international community. And, I make so bold as to repeat that this is one of the 
consequences of the management of the situation; post-Kargil mis-adventure. 
SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Sir, American sympathy for us is welcome. Also 
welcome is President Clinton's offer to"talk to Musharraf, conveying our concern. However 
this aspect has to be taken note of. On the one hand, they are supporting Pakistan 
diplomatically and financially. They are endowing Pakistan with full power in all aspects to 
wage cross-border

to say that it has never been this Government 's approach that a great country, like India, 
should depend on other countries to find a so lution for combating the challenges that we

sees that this no longer subservi ng the national interests of the United States of America or

change that has taken place. When we engage with the United States of America, we 
engage on much broader terms, in  this regard, not as if we, a great country, like India was 
somehow asking the United States to intervene in the matter.

RAJYA SABHA [3rd August, 2000] 
(a) whether it is a fact that many children (male/female) below the age of 18 years 
work as servants in both middle and high class families; 
(b) if so, the total number of such children in the country within 5 to 10 years and 11 
to 18 years age group alongwith State-wise and age-wise details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that no welfare organisation is available for them; 
(d) if so, by when Government will set-up such an organisation; and 
(e) if not, the reasons thereof or? 
THE MINISTER OF LABOUR (DR. SATYA NARAYAN JATIYA): (a) to (e) A 
statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Employment of children below the age of 14, is prohibited in 13 occupations and 
51 processes listed in the schedule to the Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 
1986. The occupations and processes considered hazardous are added to the schedule to the 
Child Labour (Prohibition & Regulation) Act, 1986 on the advice of the Technical Advisor 
Committee constituted under sections 5 of the Ac t. The schedule does not include domestic 
servants. 
(b) Authentic information on the number of working children is generated during the 
decennial census. As per the 1991 census, the total number of working children in the 
country is 1.12 crores. Figures of the number of persons working ad domestic servants are 
not maintained. 
(c) to (e) Government of India has been implementing two schemes for rehabilitation 
of children withdrawn from work, namely the scheme of National Child Labour Project 
(NCLP) and the scheme of Grant-in-aid to Voluntary Organisations. 93 NCLPS are currently 
under implementation in 11 child labour endemic states for rehabilitation of approximately 
2.00 lakh children. Government has approved continueance of the scheme of NCLP for the 
duration of the Ninth Five Year Plan and e xpansion of number of project up to 100. Under 
the Scheme of Gants-in-aid, funds are re leased to Voluntary Organisations, on the 
recommendation of the concerned State Govern ment, for taking up action oriented projects 
for the benefit of working children.

 Full deregulation of National Long Distance Operations (NLDO), before August 15,

Effect of WTO Norms on Farmers 
1242. SHRI K.C. KONDIAH: Will the Minister of AGRICULTURE be pleased to 
state whether Government would indicate the effect of the World Trade Organization norms 
on farmers of the country? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (SHRI 
S.B.P.B.K. SATYANARAYANA RAO): The Agreement on Agriculture (AOA), which is one 
of the Agreements under the World Trade Organisation (WTO), came into force from 1st 
January, 1995. The Agreement incorporates three broad areas of commitments viz., (i) 
market access i.e. the disciplines on import restraints and import tariff, (ii) domestic 
support, i.e. subsidies by Governments to dom estic farmers, and (iii) export subsidies. 
Under market access provisions, the ACA seeks to convert all non-tariff barriers such as 
Quantitative Restrictions into tariffs. The tariff levels have been bound by India for primary 
agricultural products, processed agricultural products and edible oils, with a few exceptions, 
at 100%, 150% and 300% respectively. Therefore, import of agricultural commodities into 
India can be suitably regulated by imposing appropriate tariffs within the bound levels which, 
would protect the interest of farmers. Regarding domestic support, the ACA seeks to identify 
acceptable measures of support to farmers and to limit unacceptable trade-distorting support 
to farmers. The permissible category of support includes Government assistance on general 
services, viz., (i) research, pest and disease control, training, extension, and advisory 
services, (ii) public stock holding for food s ecurity purposes, (iii) domestic food aid, and 
(iv) direct payment to produ cers like Governmental financ ial participation in income 
insurance and safety nets, relief from natural disasters, and payments under environmental 
assistance programmes. Only the Aggregate Measure of Support (AMS) comprising the 
Product specific support and Non-Product specific support given to the agricultural sector is 
subject to reduction commitments. A maximum level of AMS upto 10% of the value of 
agricultural output for developing countries, such as India, and upto 5% for developed 
countries is exempt from reduc tion commitments. AMS given to the agricultural sector in 
India is presently below the permissible maximum level of 10% of the value of agricultural 
output and, therefore, India is under no oblig ation to reduce domestic support rendered to 
the agricultural sector. India has no reducti on commitments under export subsidies since no 
such subsidies are provided by the Government. 
Food security concerns are central to the ag ricultural policy of India and the export-
import policy of agricultural products is governed principally by such concerns, the need to 
maximise farmer's income and foreign exchange

products, while at the same time protect ing, and providing avenues for rural

Preserving Cattle Wealth 
1277. SHRI LALITBHAI MEHTA: Will the Minister of AGRICUL-TURE be pleased to 
state: 
 whether it is a fact that drought animals provide 30,000 Megawatt of power, plough 100 
million hectares of land, save 6 billion tonnes of petroleum and carry more than five times freight 
and four times the passenger traffic as compared to Indian Railways in terms of originating traffic; 
 whether drought animals contribute Rs. 90,000 crores worth of output by way of milk, 
work, dung, fibre, meat and skin; and 
 what steps are taken to preserve our animal wealth and not allow them to go to 
slaughter houses? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF AGRICULTURE (DR. DEBENDRA 
PRADHAN): (a) Very little authentic data is available on utilization of animal energy. Several 
estimates put energy output of draught animals as equivalent of 30,000 megawatt and area cultivated 
by draught animals as a little less than 100 hectares. Some estimates put the savings in terms of 
diesel as 22.75 million tones per year through use of animal power. In terms of originating traffic, 
animals transport 1922.50 million tones of freight in the country while the railways carry 409.02 
million tones. However, in terms of originating passenger traffic, railways carry 4152 million numbers 
as against 360 millions carried by animals. 
70 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
 Draught animals generally produce milk in quantities sufficient only for their 
offspring. Output from draught animals in term s of milk, work, dung, fibre, meat, skin are 
not estimated separately. 
 Some of the animal species are reared  in the country exclusively for meat 
purposes. Preventing their slaughter is not contemplated at this stage. However, several 
State Government enacted legi slation relating to prevention of slaughter of cow and its 
progeny. The States of Arunachal Pradesh, Kerala, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland and 
Tripura as well as Union Territory of Lakshw adeep do not have any legislation in this 
regard. The Supreme Court has observed in variou s cases that (i) a total ban on slaughter of 
bulls and bullocks is ultra-virus the Constitutio n and (ii) an absolute ban on slaughter of 
bulls and bullocks is not necessary for comp laying with Article 48 of the Constitution. 
Besides these legislative actions, a number of schemes are implemented by the Union 
Government as well as State Governments to  preserve and develop indigenous animal 
genetic resources.

(b) The need for further streamlining the Targeted Public Distribution System (TPDS) 
with focus on better targetisation and increasing the allocation of foodgrains to families below 
Poverty Line (BPL) had been engaging the attention of Government for some time. 
Accordingly the following modifi cations with effect from 1.4. 2000 have been effected in 
the TPDS for better targetising the food s ubsidy towards enhancing the food security for 
BPL families:— 
(i) The quantity of foodgrains for BPL families under the TPDS has been doubled

allocation, if demanded by the States/UTs are also considered subject to 
availability and at economic cost.

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at farm and commercial 
level, to modernise the system  of handling, storage and transportation of the foodgrains 
procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI) and to bring in additionallity of resources 
through private sector involvement, the-Gove rnment has approved a National Policy on 
Handling, Storage and Transportation of Foodgrains, details of which are given below:— 
1. Objectives of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
(i)    to reduce storage and transit losses at farm level where about 70% of the 
total foodgrains production is retained and 
91 

RAJYA SABHA                      [3rd August, 2000] 
consumed and also to encourage the farmers to adopt scientific storage 
methods. 
(ii) to modernise the system of hand ling, storage and transportation of the 
foodgrains procured by Food Corporation of India (FCI).  
(iii) t o  h ar n es s  ef f o r t s  an d  r es o u r ces  o f  public and private sectors, both domestic 
and foreign, to build and operate infrastructure for introduction of bulk handling, 
storage and transportation of foodgrains in the country. 
2. Policy for house-hold storage 
 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the total production and 
substantial quantities of foodgrains are wasted due to improper storage at 
farm level, the major focus is on the improvement of storage standards at 
farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this need is the Save Grain 
Campaign, which popularises  the use of metallic and non-metallic storage 
structures and educates the farmer s about the adoption of s c i e n t i f i c  
storage methods. The scheme also aims at development/improvement of 
non-metallic traditional storage structures. 
 In order to have greater success in this area, following initiatives have been 
approved:— 
(i) introduction of a scheme to encourage use of metal bins as well as non-
mettalic storage structures at indivi dual farm level and construction of 
RCC bins at community level with appropriate financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training components of 
t he Save Grain Camp aign Scheme for scientific storage and 
preservation of foodgrains and their propagation among farmers. 
3. Modernisation and Upgradat ion of Bulk Grain Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is  necessary to develop and modernise the 
infrastructure for integrated bulk handling, storage and transportation in India. The 
thrust of the policy should be:— 
(i)    encouragement of mechanical harvesting, cleaning and drying at farm and 
mandi level. 
92 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(ii) transportation of grains from farm to silos by specially designed trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as distribution points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and thereafter to pre-determined 
destinations by specially designed trucks/fail wagons (with top filling and 
bottom discharge mechanism) dedicated trains. 
(v)    declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated bulk handling facilities with silos 
of large capacity for wheat along with tes ting facilities for quality control would be 
created at about 20 identified central locations in producing and consuming areas as 
well as a few port towns. These facilities, including the infrastructure for bulk 
transportation to these centres, will be created and maintained in the private sector under 
the overall co-ordination of the FCI. The design of special top filling and bottom 
discharge wagons would be decided the consultation with the Ministry of Railways. 
The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted while deciding the locations and the 
circuits where these wagons would ply. FCI will guarantee utilisation of these facilities 
to the extent of 100% for the first ten years and 75% for the next ten years. From these 
points, secondary transportation of foodgrains would be made in bag form to about 500 
godowns in important central locations in different States to be owned and 
maintained by the FCI. Further transportation to the consuming centres for retail distribution 
under the Public Distribution System will be carried out by the State Governments. 
 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage capacities in which they will 
store and maintain foodgrains procured by the Government agencies, for which 
they will be entitled to storage charges. 
 The private sector participation should be sought and encouraged for development of 
infrastructure of the integrated bulk handling, storage and transportation through— 
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Opera te-Transfer (BOOT), Build-Own-Lease-
Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Operate(BOO), Lease-Develop-
Operate(LDO), Joint Ventures etc. 
93 

RAJYA SABHA                    [3rd August, 2000] 
(ii)    generation of funds through public issues by private enterprises. 
(iii)    automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 100%. 
(iv)    loans from financial institutions, NABARD, external commercial borrowings. 
(v)    fiscal incentives as given below: 
 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income Tax for the first five 
years and 30% deduction in profit for the next five years. 
 deduction of 40% of the profits derived by financial institutions financing 
such projects, as provided to fi nancial corporations engaged, inter-alia, in 
providing long term finance for agricultural development. 
 customs duty exemption for items not ma nufactured in India, on a case-to-
case basis, subject to a list of such equipment being submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, therefore, the infrastructure 
facilities available at the ports are basica lly meant for unloading operations and not for 
exports. For unloading operations, ship gears are normally used. Even the latest 
mechanised facilities at Jawaharlal Nehru Po rt, Navi Mumbai have been designed for 
import purposes only. There is also lack of general cargo berths at the major ports and 
very limited warehousing facilities are availabl e for the storage of foodgrains at ports. 
For creating the proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due course, the 
infrastructure facilities would have to be  developed for which following actions are 
required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of export of foodgrains. The 
distribution of foodgrains traffic may spread over to the non-traditional ports which 
have spare capacity like New Mangalore and Cochin ports; 
(ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports through ports, own 
investment/private participation; 
94 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iii) water front/berths can be leased to the users who may be encouraged to put 
up their own facilities; and 
(iv) development of dedicated modern f oodgrains handling faci lities at selected 
ports. 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
 facilitate speedy clearance of projects concerning development of 
infrastructure for bulk handling, transportation and storage of foodgrains by 
setting up an Approval Board competent to take final decision; 
 enter into bilateral agreem ents with other countries/ international agencies 
for p r o v i d i n g  technical/financial assistance; 
 take necessary legislative/administrative measures for removing impediments 
with regard to stock control Orders /movement control Orders framed by 
various State Governments; 
 utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory mechanism for 
fixing/regulating tariff for various ope rations, such as cleaning, drying, 
storage, transportation etc.; 
 make available facilities of the Railways for bulk transporatation; 
 promote negotiable Ware house Receipt System by which farmers could 
hold their grains back from market and meet their working capital/short 
term requirement by borrowing from banks against these receipts; and 
 promote research for development of alternate storage technologies like 
Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) technology which would ensure longer 
shelf life of foodgrains and help export of foodgrains in vacuum packs. 
6. Role of the State Government 
The State Government would help in: 
(a)    acquisition of land required for various projects as for public purpose; and 
95 

RAJYA SABHA                        [3rd August, 2000] 
(b)    making available other facilities such as water, power, road, etc.

Statement-II 
Main Recommendations of the Working Group on Information Technology 
for Masses 
The Working Group on "IT for Masses", has recommended that 
 Government should facilitate establishment of onc million IT Kiosks, with 
useful Government and private content available on revenue sharing basis. 
 Take up immediate programme to estab lish IT education infrastructure in 
60,000 schools. 
 Launch Mass Awareness Campaign through IT Yatras and other programmes. 
 Set up specific time table for Web-enabled Citizen Oriented Government 
Services; and 
 Set up 'IT Mission" for 5 years to carry out this focussed programme. 
The theme on which the report revolves, is that IT can be effective tool of 
"Empowering people" in real sense. To achieve this objective, it is necessary 
121 

RAJYA SABHA                                 [3rd August, 2000] 
to provide "Easy Access at affordable rates". "1 million IT Kiosk by 2005" will be the model to 
reach out to the masses who can not afford PC and Internet. The theme of the Working Group 
emphasizes that spread of IT is possible if IT infrastructure penetrates to schools, at the earliest. 
Government must develop Web-centric Citizen Oriented applications and make it available on 
Public Access System. Mass awareness Campaign is needed to make public aware of the immense 
benefits of the IT revolution. All these efforts will ensure "Digital Unite" rather than "Digital 
Divide". 
The other major recommendations are, mat mile connectivity should be franchised on 
revenue sharing model, private E-Com information infrastructures should be allowed CUG 
status, promote indigenous technology for low cost Internet access devices and Indian language 
development, Right of Way should be granted cable operators also. On E-Governance front the 
Working Group has recommended that Centre and States should prepare five year IT Plans and 
keep 5% of the budget for this which will ensure more productive and efficient use of remaining 
95% of the budget; take immediate steps for sensitization of decision makers, standardize formats 
and procedures by setting up Administrative Re-engineering Commission; make sure that IT 
infrastructure is in place at working level staff by 200.1 and set up time table for citizen oriented 
applications to go on Web. 
The Group has recommended that 60,000 schools in 6000 blocks, should have minimum lOPC 
infrasturcture  in place in five year time frame. This is possible through joint efforts of Centre and State 
Governments, industry, NGOs, donors, NRIs and schools themselves. Central Government can either provide 
10% of the cost or provide free Internet, useful appliances, CDs and Teachers training. 
The Group has also suggested a new scheme  called "Antyodaya Computer Literacy 
Programme". One lakh youths from SC/ST/BPL will be provided IT foundation course in this 
scheme every year for next five years. 
In a novel scheme, the Woking Group has suggested that IT YATRA should be organised 
between January, 2001 to February, 2001 from four comers of the country, demonstrating "benefits of 
IT in empowering people". Various competitions and National IT talent search are other 
programmes of the recommended package. 
The Group has recommended setting up of "IT Mission" for focussed follow up on all 
these measures for the period of next five years.

INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (SHRI PRAMOD MAHAJAN): (a) and (b) Subsidiaries 
of Indian Software Companies doing busine ss in Japan are being subjected to 20% 
withholding tax on the payments made to the pa rent company in India. These payments are

law for them. The consultation process is yet to be completed with a consensus on the issue. 
The proposed Bill would be introduced as soon as a consensus is emerged in the matter. 
Statement 
Text of the speech made by Minister of Labour, Andhra Pradesh In 1LC in June, 
2000. 
I am grateful to the president for giving me this opportunity to lend the support of our 
country to the cause of health and safety of agricultural workers. As you may know, we have 
the largest population of agricultural workers in our country, approximately 150 million, and we 
are committed as a nation and as a Government to their welfare, health and safety. The initiative 
taken by the ILO 
135 

RAJYA SABHA                            [3rd August, 2000] 
to formulate international instruments, that is a convention supplemented by a 
Recommendation, on health and safety for agricultural workers is both timely and 
commendable. Agricultural work activities range over a very large spectrum, from the most 
modern farms and plantations to those undertak en by small, medium-sized and marginal 
farmers, and even sharecroppers, squatters and indigenous people. The ILO has estimated 
that there are about 1.3 billion workers enga ged in agricultural production worldwide, and 
there are about 170,000 fatal workplace casualties among such workers annually. This 
sector is also assessed as one of the thre e most accident-prone, along with mining and 
construction. Therefore, the need to provide pr otection and safety to such workers is self-
evident. In developing countries, most of th e holdings are small and medium-sized, and 
often the whole family is engaged in agricu ltural activities. Generally, such workers are 
poor, have little education, suffer from malnutrition, and are v i ct ims of chronic ill health. 
They also lack access to social and health care services. Many of them migrate from poor 
environmentaly and economically  disadvantaged regions to seek job opportunities in more 
prosperous ones. Some of them migrate through contractors. All of them are exposed to 
various kinds of trauma, such as social excl usion and exploitation by ruthless employers. 
In India, we have about 150 million agricult ural workers who generally belong to the 
poorest and the most disadvantaged strata of society. Their working and l ivi ng  conditions 
are covered under various labour laws such as the Workers' Compensation Act, 1923, the 
Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Plantations Labour Act, 1951,  the Employment Provident 
Fund and Miscellaneous Provisi ons Act, 1952, the Insecticides Act, 1968, the labour 
C o n t r a c t  Regulation a n d  Abolition A c t ,  1 9 7 0 ,  t h e  E q u a l  R e m u n e r a t i o n s  A c t ,  1976, the 
Interstate Migrant Workers Act, 1979, the Dangerous Missions Regulations Act, 1983 and 
the Child Labour Prohibition Abolition Act, 1983, etc. 
Many of these laws have provisions for the health and safety of agricultural 
workers,but clearly much more needs to be done. With a view to providing social protection 
and welfare measures for agricultural workers in India, we have been engaged for some time 
now in the task of formulating a comprehensive law for them. We therefore welcome this 
step taken by the ILO. The provisions of the ILO instrument are sufficiently 
comprehensive, and when implemented will no doubt bring much relief to large numbers of 
workers worldwide, as indeed it will for the m ajority of workers of rural India. I t  is  th er ef or e 
a matter of satisfaction that the Committee on Safety and Health in Agriculture has concluded 
its first discussion and has come out with draft conclusions on the subject. 
136 

[3rd August, 2000] RAJYA  SABHA 
While recognizing that some of t h e  st andards may pose difficulties for some 
developing countries wishing to ratify such a convention, we still strongly s upport this 
proposal, which will do much to ensure a heal thy and safe workplace in the agricultural 
sector.

eligible for the facility of being re-deployed through the Central (Surplus Staff) Cell located

account the aforesaid addition is not more  than the service he/she could have

four broad categories:— 
 Reduction of Revenue Deficit 
 Disinvestment programmes in non-essential sectors.

ban on providing loan/share capital to Public Sector Undertakings), (ii) Increase 
in tax revenue (through levy of new entry tax, rationalisation of the tax structure 
and intensive drive to recover arrears of government dues and arrest leakages of 
revenues), (Hi) increase in non-tax revenue (through revision of fees of 
engineering colleges ft hospital rates and revision of Nazul rates), (iv) revision of 
user charges for various economic and social services.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Reported Leptospirosis outbreak in Maharashtra and Gujarat 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (DR. C.P. THAKUR): 
Recently, practitioners from North-west of Mumbai and adjacent area from Thane District 
(Malad-Virar) as weff as from Central part of Thane district (Kalyan),. reported increase in 
fever with a typical feature like bleeding and hepato-renal failure with involvement of lungs 
and high mortality. The practitioners from Mumbai suspecte'd Leptospirosis. Immediately 
concerned officers from the State visited the places and carried out the basic investigation, 
including entomological studies and gave directions regarding control. 
To meet the crisis a meeting of officers from Health Services, Medical Education 
and Research and Municipal Corporations wa s convened in the Directorate of Health 
Services, Mumbai on 29 th July, 2000. The possibilities  considered   for   increased  fever   
cases   were   Leptospirosis,

Dengue Fever and P.falciparum. Technical guidelines for labo ratory investigations and 
treatment were given al! over the State. Medical Teams were formed to assess the extent of 
the outbreak, which have been functioning in th e field. The State level rapid response team 
alongwith team from National Institute of Virology. Pune has already carried out

Leptospirosis is a zoonotic bacterial diseas e caused by leptospires of which there 
are many sero-groups and serovars. A number of leptospirosis outbreaks have been reported 
in India in the past namely; Andaman & Nicobar Islands. Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala and 
Tamil Nadu. It causes a wide variety of clin ical manifestations. Jaundice and haemorrhagic 
manifestations are present in typical cases. At times cases may be misdiagnosed as viral 
fever, dengue haemorrhagic fever, malaria, etc. 
Mode of transmission 
Contact with skin (with cuts and bruises) and mucous membrane with water soil 
or vegetation contaminated with urine of infected animals like rats, pigs, cattle, dogs, etc.   
leads to infection in man,

Treatment and Prevention 
Specific treatment with anti-microbials is effective if started early in the course of illness. 
Penicillin, cephalosporins, doxycycline, erythromycin are all effective. Preventive measures 
includes elimination or minimization of human contact with contaminated water, soil or 
vegetation. Proper protective clothing such as boots and gloves are recommended in areas 
where risk is perceived to be high. 
Diagnosis is based on serological tests an d Isolation of leptosplrosis from the blood 
and urine. Facilities for serological disease are available with NICD, MICR and several medical 
institutions including State Government hospitals and medical colleges. 
On the direction of the Director General, Indian Council of Medical Research 
(ICMR), Director, Regional Medical Research Centre, Port Blair has reached Mumbai to help in 
carrying out investigations to confirm the di agnosis. A team from National Institute of 
Communicable Diseases has also been deputed to assist the State Health Authorities in 
containment and investigation. 
The Central Government is seized of  the matter and dosely monitoring the 
situation. 
All Central assistance required and considered necessary will be provided to the State 
Government.
